summary: A Network Host Status report covering May 22 to June 2, 1972. No testing was done on Memorial Day or on May 31 and June 1, because of an attempt to install the new IMP system. Three new terminal IMPs were installed during the period. It was replaced by RFC 362.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

subtitle: Checking which network hosts were working in late May and early June 1972

tldr.problem: Users needed current status of ARPANET host availability as the network continued to expand.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested network hosts from May 22 to June 2, 1972. Three new Terminal IMPs were installed during this period at Fort Belvoir, SAAC, and NOAA.
tldr.outcome: The report shows continued network growth with new Terminal IMP sites coming online, expanding access to the network.

today: RFC 362 replaced this status report in June 1972. The new Terminal IMP locations expanded ARPANET access beyond major research computing centers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 353 reports on host status from May 22 to June 2, 1972. During this period, three new Terminal IMPs were installed: Terminal IMP #155 at Fort Belvoir in Virginia (June 1), Terminal IMP #154 at SAAC (Seismic Array Analysis Center) in Alexandria, Virginia (June 3), and Terminal IMP #153 at NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) in Boulder, Colorado (June 5). No testing was done on May 29 (Memorial Day) or May 31 and June 1 (due to an attempt to install the new IMP system).
sections.plainLanguage: Three new locations got Terminal IMPs, which let more organizations connect to the network. The ARPANET team was also working on upgrading the main switching equipment.

sections.title: Host Categories
sections.content:
By June 1972, the excluded category included Terminal IMPs (now at AMES, MITRE, NBS, ETAC, USC, GWC, NOAA, SAAC, BELVOIR, and BBN) and the Network Control Center (Address 5). The only non-server host excluded was the PDP-10 at Case (Address 13), still expected to become a server.

The operational servers remained the major universities and research centers: UCLA, SRI, UCSB, UTAH, MIT (three sites), RAND, SDC, Harvard, Lincoln, Stanford, Carnegie, and AMES, forming the backbone of the early ARPANET.
sections.plainLanguage: New Terminal IMPs let smaller offices and agencies connect to the network without their own big computer. Most of the big research computers were already set up to share.

sections.title: Status Patterns
sections.content:
The testing results show varying reliability across the network. Some machines like SRI-NIC, UCSB, MIT-Multics, and Harvard were consistently Open. Others like SRI-AI remained dead throughout the period. Some hosts like AMES-67 were dead every single day, indicating systematic failures that persisted across several months.

The network showed the typical challenges of early distributed computing: intermittent connectivity issues, regularly scheduled downtime for system work, and varying implementation maturity across different host sites.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers worked reliably every day. Others were broken almost all the time. Some were sometimes up and sometimes down. Building a network across many different computers was hard.
